15.title: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help"
15.hook: the hinge of the prayer: it turns from talking about God to talking to God, and it says one
15.howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in every unit of every prayer. Tawhid is the heart of Muslim belief, said in the shahada, and many Muslims raise the index finger of the right hand when they bear witness in the sitting part of the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yawm ad-din, the day every account is settled. Your line was the account is in kind hands. Today, the prayer turns around. Day fifteen.
screen: `YAWM AD-DIN — THE ACCOUNT IS IN KIND HANDS.` → `DAY 15.`

segments.voice: Mecca, in the early years. A man named Bilal is enslaved there, and he has become a Muslim. The early biographies say the man who owned him would drag him out into the noon heat, lay him on the burning sand, put a heavy rock on his chest, and tell him to give up his faith. And Bilal, crushed under the stone, would say only one word, over and over. Ahad. Ahad. One. One. He comes back in two days, as the voice of the call to prayer. Today, his word, and the verse where al-Fatiha says it.

Verse five: “Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help.” In Arabic, iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in. Two things happen here. First, the prayer turns around. For four verses it has talked about God: praise be to Him, the Merciful, the Owner of the Day. Now, suddenly, it talks to God. You. In the conversation from day two, God's answer changes here too: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked. Second, listen to the order of the Arabic. It doesn't say we worship You. It says You, we worship. Putting You first makes it exclusive: only You, and only You for help. That's today's word in miniature. Tawhid. The root is w-h-d, one; wahid is the number one. Tawhid means making one, affirming one. It's the first half of the shahada from day nine: there is no god but God. It even has its own surah, four lines long, that opens: “Say: He is Allah, the One!” Here's why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. If God is one, everything else, however big it looms, isn't God. Your job, your phone, your fear, other people's opinion of you: real, and none of them ultimate. One way to put tawhid: one center, instead of a dozen. That's what Bilal was saying under the rock. Not an argument. The center, holding.
screen: `THE PRAYER TURNS: ABOUT GOD, TO GOD.` · `YOU, WE WORSHIP — YOU ALONE.` · `W-H-D — ONE.` · `ONE CENTER, NOT A DOZEN.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and gather your attention into one place: the breath at the tip of your nose. Just that. When your mind splits off into a dozen places, the list, the text, the worry, notice it, and bring it back to the one breath. Again and again. In the prayer, at the words of witness, many raise one finger of the right hand; you can rest one finger up while you sit, if you like. If you pray, let the word rest there: ahad.
Tawhid. The oneness of God, affirmed: You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help. Fifteenth word.
Your line: one. One center, instead of a dozen things pulling at you. Day fifteen.

16.title: "Show us the straight path"
16.hook: the whole prayer is a request for directions, and the road has footprints on it
16.tomorrow: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
16.howItsDone: Muslims ask for the straight path in every unit of every prayer, and then recite verse seven to close al-Fatiha. Many also use the phrase in their own prayers, asking to be guided in a decision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawhid, You alone. Your line was simply one. Today, al-Fatiha finally asks for something. Day sixteen.

Think about the last time you were properly lost. Not a little turned around. Lost. The phone at two percent, the street signs in a language you can't read, every corner looking like the one before. What did you finally do? You stopped someone and asked: which way? It's a humbling question. And at the center of the prayer Muslims say most, after praise and mercy and trust, the one thing it asks for is directions.
screen: `PROPERLY LOST.` → `WHICH WAY?` → `THE PRAYER ASKS FOR DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Verse six: “Show us the straight path.” In Arabic, ihdina s-sirata l-mustaqim. One word at a time. Ihdina: show us, guide us, from the root h-d-y, the same root as hidaya, guidance, and as hadiya, a gift. Guidance, in this language, is something handed to you. Sirat is a road, a wide, clear way. Mustaqim: straight, upright, not bending. Together, today's word: as-sirat al-mustaqim, the straight path. Notice the small word us. Even someone praying completely alone, at three in the morning, says show us. Then verse seven says whose path it is: “The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray.” Not an abstract rule, then, but a road with footprints on it. Another verse names those favored as the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous: the best of company. And two ways of missing it, which one common reading hears as knowing the way and walking off it, and never finding it at all. Muslims who pray ask for this road many times a day, for a lifetime. Why keep asking for a road you're already on? A simple answer: the path isn't found once. You ask to be shown it, and kept on it, at every corner. That's all seven verses, walked.
screen: `IHDINA — SHOW US, A GIFT.` · `SIRAT — A WIDE, CLEAR ROAD.` · `A ROAD WITH FOOTPRINTS ON IT.` · `ASKED AGAIN AT EVERY CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one place in your life where you honestly don't know which way to go: a decision, a relationship, a next step. Don't solve it. Stand at that corner for a moment and admit you don't know. Then picture one person who walked a hard road well, and the way they carried themselves. If you pray, you can carry the line in Arabic or English: show us the straight path.
As-sirat al-mustaqim. The straight path: a wide, clear road, asked for in every prayer, with footprints on it. Sixteenth word.
Your line: show us the way. Even praying alone, the prayer says us, not me. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS. AL-FATIHA, ALL SEVEN VERSES.` → `TOMORROW: THE CALL TO PRAYER, AND WHY IT'S BEAUTIFUL.`

17.title: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
17.hook: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
17.howItsDone: In Muslim-majority places a mu'adhdhin gives the adhan from the mosque, often by loudspeaker, at each of the five prayer times; elsewhere it's often heard from an app, and in many families it's said softly into a newborn's ear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: as-sirat al-mustaqim, the straight path, and the last of al-Fatiha's seven verses. Your line was show us the way. Today, the call that brings people to the prayer. Day seventeen.

Before dawn, in a city still dark, one voice starts up from a minaret. A single voice, rising, holding a note longer than seems possible, then falling away. Then a second voice, farther off, a beat behind. Then another. For a few minutes the rooftops are full of the same words, never quite in sync. It isn't a song, exactly, and it isn't an alarm. It's an invitation, sent out at each of the five prayer times.
screen: `ONE VOICE, HOLDING A NOTE.` → `THEN ANOTHER, A BEAT BEHIND.` → `WHAT IS IT SAYING?`

segments.voice: The adhan. Its root, a-dh-n, is the root of the ear, udhun: the call is literally the thing you hear. In the first years in Medina, the sayings report, the young community didn't have one. People gathered by guessing the time. The companions talked it over: a bell? A horn? A fire? Then a companion named Abdullah ibn Zayd dreamed of a man teaching him the words. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said it was a true dream, and told him: teach it to Bilal, his voice carries. Bilal is the man from day fifteen, saying ahad, one, under the rock. By now he was free, and his voice called the city to prayer. The words: Allahu akbar, God is greater. Then two witnesses: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Then the heart of it. Hayya 'ala s-salah: come to prayer. Hayya 'ala l-falah: come to success. Falah is flourishing, and its root is the root of the farmer, the one who splits the ground so something can grow. At dawn, Sunni callers add a line: prayer is better than sleep. The Shia call carries a line of its own at every prayer: come to the best of deeds. That's why it can be beautiful even without the Arabic. Its whole job is to turn toward you and say: come. You, now.
screen: `ADHAN — FROM THE ROOT FOR EAR.` · `A DREAM, AND BILAL'S VOICE.` · `COME TO PRAYER. COME TO SUCCESS.` · `COME. YOU, NOW.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen. Not to anything in particular: just to what's calling right now. A car outside, the fridge, your own breathing, someone's voice in another room. Each one is asking for a little of your attention. Notice what you turn toward. If you pray, you can let the old words sit under the sound: come to prayer, come to success.
The adhan. The call to prayer, from the root for ear. God is greater; come to prayer; come to success. Seventeenth word.
Your line: you are being called. Come to prayer, come to flourishing, said to you. Day seventeen.

18.title: friday
18.hook: Friday; why the week has a hinge
18.howItsDone: On Fridays, many Muslims bathe, dress well and go to the mosque at midday for the khutbah and a two-unit congregational prayer that replaces the noon prayer, then return to work or school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the adhan. Your line was you are being called. Today, the one call a week that gathers everyone. Day eighteen.

Just after noon on a Friday. A cab driver parks and locks the car. A nurse swaps her shift. A young guy slips out of the office in a borrowed tie. A shopkeeper pulls the shutter halfway down. They're all walking the same way, and the sidewalk outside the mosque fills until people are praying on mats laid out on the street. An hour later they're all walking back, and the city picks up exactly where it left off.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST AFTER NOON.` → `EVERYONE WALKING ONE WAY.` → `THEN BACK TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Jumu'ah. The Arabic name for Friday comes from the root j-m-', to gather. The same root gives jami', the big gathering mosque, and jama'ah, the congregation. Friday is, literally, gathering day. The Qur'an sets it up in a surah named after it: “When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading.” Leave your trading. Stop the sale, close the laptop. But listen to the next verse: “And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty.” Go back to work. So Friday isn't a day off. It's a hinge: the week swings on it for an hour, then carries on. What happens in that hour? A sermon, the khutbah, given in two parts, and then a prayer of two units that takes the place of the usual noon prayer. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught the preparation too: wash the whole body, wear your best, put on perfume, come early. One of his sayings calls Friday the best day the sun rises on, the day Adam was created. Another says there's an hour on Friday when any prayer is answered, and nobody knows exactly which hour. The schools work out the details of who must attend and when. The point is in the name: once a week, you show up, together.
screen: `JUMU'AH — FROM A ROOT FOR GATHERING.` · `LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `THEN GO BACK TO WORK.` · `ONCE A WEEK, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Think of the people you actually gather with. A family table, a team, a group chat, a few friends at the same café. Picture their faces, one at a time. Notice who you haven't gathered with in a long while. Let one name come up and stay. If you pray, you can remember them in it. If you don't, just hold their face a little longer.
Jumu'ah. Friday, gathering day: a sermon and a prayer at noon, then back to work. The hinge of the week. Eighteenth word.
Your line: gather. Once a week the city bends around it, then carries on. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PILLAR THAT'S ABOUT MONEY.`

19.title: the pillar that's about money
19.hook: the pillar that's about money; 2.5% and why
19.carry: what you give purifies what you keep
19.tomorrow: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
19.howItsDone: Muslims whose savings are above the nisab threshold calculate zakat once a lunar year, usually 2.5 percent, and give it to people in the categories the Qur'an names, often through a mosque or charity; many time it for Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jumu'ah, gathering day. Your line was gather. Today, the pillar about a bank balance. Day nineteen.

Five pillars hold up a Muslim life. One is a statement of faith, one is prayer, one is fasting, one is a journey. And one is about a bank balance. Not a general hope that people will be generous: a number, worked out once a year like a tax return, with a calculator or a pencil at the kitchen table. Mosques post online calculators for it. It can look like paperwork. And its name means something close to purity.
screen: `FIVE PILLARS, ONE ABOUT MONEY.` → `A NUMBER, ONCE A YEAR.` → `ITS NAME MEANS PURITY.`

segments.voice: Zakat. Its root, z-k-w, holds two ideas at once: to be pure, and to grow. It's like pruning a plant. You cut some away, and what's left is cleaner, and grows better. The Qur'an names prayer and zakat together again and again: “Establish worship, pay the poor-due.” God and neighbor in one breath. How does it work? Once a lunar year, a Muslim whose savings stay above a set threshold, the nisab, traditionally measured in gold or silver, gives a share of that wealth. The early rules set it, for silver, at a quarter of a tenth: one fortieth, two and a half percent. Not of income: of what you've held on to for a year. Why so small? One way to read it: it's sized so anyone above the line can give it every year without being ruined by it, so it never stops. Where does it go? The Qur'an names eight kinds of people, starting with the poor and the needy, and including people crushed by debt and the stranded traveler. And it speaks of a known right in people's wealth for the one who asks and the one who goes without. So the money isn't framed as the giver's gift. It's a right, already inside the wealth, being handed back. Shia practice adds khums, a fifth of the year's surplus. And beyond all of it is sadaqa, giving from the heart, any amount, anytime. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ counted even a smile at your brother as sadaqa.
screen: `ZAKAT — TO PURIFY, TO GROW.` · `PRAYER AND ZAKAT, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `TWO AND A HALF PERCENT, ONCE A YEAR.` · `THE POOR'S RIGHT, HANDED BACK.`

segments.voice: Think about what you have right now. Not only money: time this week, food in the kitchen, a skill, a coat you haven't worn in two years. Let one thing come to mind that you've held on to longer than you need. Picture the pruning: that one thing cut away and handed on. Notice how the rest of what you have feels after it. Lighter, or heavier? Just notice.
Zakat. The third pillar: two and a half percent of savings, given once a year, from a root meaning to purify and to grow. Nineteenth word.
Your line: what you give purifies what you keep. Like pruning: less, and it grows better. Day nineteen.

screen: `DAY 19 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AN ORPHAN, A MERCHANT, A MAN WHO WAS TRUSTED BEFORE HE WAS BELIEVED.`

20.title: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
20.hook: an orphan, a merchant, a man who was trusted before he was believed
20.howItsDone: Muslims say "peace be upon him" (or write ﷺ) after the Prophet's name, never picture him, and learn his life, the sira, from the Qur'an, the hadith and the early biographies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat. Your line was what you give purifies what you keep. Today, the man at the center of it all. Day twenty.
screen: `ZAKAT — WHAT YOU GIVE PURIFIES WHAT YOU KEEP.` → `DAY 20.`

segments.voice: Who holds the spare key to your home? Probably not the most impressive person you know. The most trustworthy one, the one who has never once let you down. The early biographies say a whole city felt that way about one man. Clans who'd fight over a camel all agreed on him, and gave him a nickname for it. Years later, many of those same people refused to believe what he told them, and still left their valuables in his care. Today, told the way Islam tells him: in words only.
screen: `WHO HOLDS YOUR SPARE KEY?` → `A WHOLE CITY TRUSTED ONE MAN.` → `TRUSTED, NOT YET BELIEVED.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, peace be upon him. In Muslim tradition he isn't drawn or pictured; he's known through words, so words are all we'll use. The early biographies say he was born in Mecca, around the year 570. His father died before he was born, his mother when he was six, and the grandfather who took him in two years later. His uncle Abu Talib raised him after that. So when the Qur'an speaks to him, it can say: “Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?” He grew up herding sheep, then traveled with the trade caravans. A merchant and widow named Khadijah hired him to lead hers, and was so struck by his honesty that she proposed marriage. By then Mecca had a name for him: al-Amin, the trustworthy. The biographies tell a story about it. The clans were rebuilding the Ka'ba and nearly came to blows over who would set the sacred Black Stone back in its place. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was him. He spread out a cloak, set the stone on it, and had a man from each clan lift a corner, together. At forty, he began to receive the Qur'an. A saying records how he stood on a hill and asked his people: if I told you an army was behind this hill, would you believe me? We've never known you to lie, they said. Then he told them his message, and many turned away. Trusted first. Believed, by many, only later.
screen: `AN ORPHAN IN MECCA.` · `A MERCHANT, AND KHADIJAH.` · `AL-AMIN — AND THE BLACK STONE.` · `WE'VE NEVER KNOWN YOU TO LIE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who trusts you with something. A secret, a key, a child, a job. Picture them handing it over, and notice what it feels like to be trusted. Then think of one small promise you've made lately and haven't kept yet. Nothing dramatic: a call, a book to return, a message you said you'd send. Just hold it. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it.
The Prophet, peace be upon him. An orphan, a shepherd, a merchant, called al-Amin, the trustworthy, long before most believed him. Twentieth word.
Your line: al-Amin, the trustworthy. He was trusted first, and believed by many only later. Day twenty.

21.title: the short surahs
21.hook: the short surahs; the mountain ahead
21.carry: the ones every Muslim child knows
21.tomorrow: The one who would be a steward
21.howItsDone: Muslim children usually begin memorizing the Qur'an from the end, with the short surahs of juz' 'amma, and these are the surahs most often recited in the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prophet, peace be upon him, al-Amin, the trustworthy. Now the whole camp, quickly: bismillah, al-Fatiha, wudu, inshallah, iman, Ramadan, Eid, salaam, the five pillars, salat, alhamdulillah, Rabb, rahma, yawm ad-din, tawhid, as-sirat al-mustaqim, the adhan, Jumu'ah, zakat, the Prophet. Twenty words. Today makes twenty-one.

Twenty words: the everyday vocabulary of a Muslim life. That's the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing, into the stories of the prophets, one after another. So today, from the top of the foothills, look up at the mountain itself, the Qur'an, and find the place where almost every Muslim starts to climb it. Oddly enough, it's at the very end.
screen: `THE FOOTHILLS, DONE.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.` → `START AT THE END.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an has a hundred and fourteen surahs, roughly longest first, shortest last. To make it possible to read the whole thing in a month, especially in Ramadan, it's divided into thirty equal parts. Each part is a juz'. The last one is called juz' 'amma, after its very first word. Surah seventy-eight opens: “Whereof do they question one another?” In Arabic, 'amma yatasa'alun. So 'amma, whereof, names the whole part. It holds the surahs from seventy-eight to the end. Most are short, some only three or four lines, and many scholars place most of them among the earliest revelations in Mecca: vivid, rhythmic, full of oaths by the dawn, the night, the fig. And this is where children begin. Not at page one: at the back. After al-Fatiha, a child often learns an-Nas, the last surah, then al-Falaq, then al-Ikhlas, the surah of oneness from day fifteen, and on backward from there. These are the surahs most often recited in the daily prayers, for a lifetime. Grandparents and five-year-olds know the same ones by heart. For some, the climb goes on for years, until the whole Qur'an is held in memory; someone who does that is called a hafiz, a keeper. But almost everyone starts here, at the small end of the mountain.
screen: `THIRTY PARTS, FOR A MONTH.` · `'AMMA — WHEREOF DO THEY QUESTION?` · `CHILDREN START AT THE BACK.` · `THE SMALL END OF THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Think back over these three weeks. Let the words drift past: the name before a beginning, the opening, the water, the fast, the feast, the greeting, the one. Don't try to remember all of them. Just notice which one has stuck, which one came back to you on an ordinary day, in the kitchen or the car, without being asked. Hold that one word. It's yours now.
Juz' 'amma. The thirtieth part of the Qur'an, the short surahs, where nearly everyone begins. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.
Your line: the ones every Muslim child knows. Tomorrow the path starts climbing, and the stories begin.
